title: Permanent establishment
summary: Article 5 decides when a business from one State has a taxable presence (a permanent establishment, PE) in the other. The Commentary covers the fixed-place test, construction sites, the preparatory and auxiliary exceptions, agents, subsidiaries, servers and the services alternative. The 2025 update added guidance on cross-border work from home (paragraphs 44.1 to 44.21) and a new optional provision for extractive industries (paragraphs 170 to 203).
readingNote: Most Saudi treaties add UN-style rules to this Article: a services PE (more than 183 days or 6 months in a 12-month period), a shorter construction threshold, and sometimes insurance and stock-agent rules. Those rules are not in the OECD Model, so this Commentary does not cover them. The UN Model notes in the Other countries tab do. The fixed-place, agency and preparatory-or-auxiliary guidance below still applies to the parts of the Saudi wording that match the OECD text.

entries.t: The PE concept mainly decides whether a State can tax the business profits of an enterprise of the other State. Under Article 7 it cannot, unless the business is carried on through a PE located there.

Independent professional services used to have their own Article (14) and the 'fixed base' concept. Article 14 was removed in 2000 because the two concepts were never meant to differ, so the PE definition now covers what used to be a fixed base.

Changes made to this Commentary in 2017 that clarify meaning also apply to older treaties. The BEPS Action 7 changes (new paragraph 4.1 and revised paragraphs 4, 5 and 6 of the Article) apply only going forward and do not change how the earlier wording is read.
Registering for VAT or GST in a State is irrelevant to whether a PE exists, and no inference should be drawn from it.

sections.heading: Paragraph 1: the fixed place of business test

entries.t: The general definition needs a distinct place, a 'fixed place of business', with three elements: a place of business, a degree of permanence at a particular location, and the enterprise's business being carried on through it, usually by its personnel.
The place need not contribute to profits directly. Every part of an enterprise is taken to contribute to the whole, so there is no requirement of 'productive character'.
Whether a PE exists in a period depends on the facts in that period. Earlier or later arrangements, for example before a business model changed, are not the test.
Whether a PE exists is decided separately from which Article taxes the profits. A farm or a rental office run by a non-resident can be a PE even if its income falls under Article 6.

A 'place of business' is any premises, facilities or installations used for the business, owned or rented, used exclusively or not. Even a certain amount of space at the enterprise's disposal is enough, including space inside another enterprise's premises.

No formal legal right to the place is needed, but mere presence at a location does not put it at the enterprise's disposal. That depends on the enterprise's effective power to use the place, how much it is present there, and what it does there. An exclusive legal right to a place used only for the enterprise's own business will usually be enough. Intermittent or incidental use of someone else's premises is not.

Four examples of working at another enterprise's premises. A salesman who regularly visits a customer's purchasing director has no PE there. An employee allowed for a long period to use an office at another company's headquarters to monitor contract compliance has that office at the employer's disposal. A haulier using a customer's delivery dock every day for years, and a painter working three days a week for two years in a client's building, both have a PE.
'Through which' is read widely: it covers any situation where business is carried on at a location at the enterprise's disposal for that purpose.
'Fixed' requires a link between the place of business and a specific geographical point. Equipment can be fixed even without being attached to the ground, as long as it stays at one site.

Activities that move between nearby locations form a single place of business only if the area is both commercially and geographically coherent. A mine qualifies, but a small area with no commercial coherence, such as unrelated clients in one district, does not. A single project spread over separate locations may also lack geographic coherence: a consultant training staff at several bank branches has a separate place at each branch.

A ship moving in international waters or between States is not fixed, unless it operates only within an area that is commercially and geographically coherent. Shops and restaurants on board are treated the same way, although paragraph 5 may apply where contracts are concluded within a State.

A PE can exist only in a State's territory. No member accepts that a geostationary satellite is located in a State's territory, and the satellite's reception 'footprint' is not at the operator's disposal.

Permanence: a place used only temporarily is not a PE. In practice States generally have not found a PE where the business was carried on at a place for less than six months, subject to the two exceptions that follow.
Recurring activities: where a place is used for short periods repeatedly over years, each period is considered together with how often the place is used.

A business carried on only in that country can be a PE despite a short duration, because its link with the country is stronger. Example: an individual who rents her parents' house in a remote village to a film crew for a four-month shoot.
Tax administrations may use these practices when resolving disagreements about whether a place is merely temporary.
Temporary interruptions do not end a PE, and a place used for very short periods but regularly over a long time is not merely temporary.

Rotating short uses of the same place among similar businesses run by the same or related persons, to keep each below the time threshold, is treated like the contract-splitting abuse described in paragraphs 52 and 53.

A place meant for short use that in fact lasts longer becomes a fixed place of business and can be a PE retrospectively. A place set up to be permanent can be a PE from the start even if special circumstances, such as death or a failed investment, end it early.
The business must be carried on wholly or partly through the place. The activity need not be productive or uninterrupted, but it must be carried on regularly.

Leasing property such as facilities, equipment, buildings or intangibles to third parties through a fixed place of business generally makes that place a PE. Leasing without such a place does not make the leased asset itself a PE, even if the lessor supplies staff to operate it, provided their role is limited to operating or maintaining it under the lessee's direction.
Container leasing has special features and is dealt with in a separate OECD report.
A telecom operator whose customers roam on another operator's network does not have that network at its disposal, so it has no PE there.
Business is usually carried on through the entrepreneur or its personnel: employees and others who take instructions from it, such as dependent agents.

Where work is done by subcontractors, a PE needs the work to be done at a fixed place at the enterprise's disposal, tested under paragraph 12. Without the enterprise's own employees there, this must be shown in another way. Profit attribution is a separate question.
Automatic equipment such as gaming or vending machines can be a PE if the enterprise operates and maintains it itself, but not if it only sets up the machines and leases them out.

'Enterprise' covers any business form carried on by a resident. Enterprises working together on one project usually each carry on their own part. Whether they form a separate enterprise, such as a partnership, depends on the facts and domestic law.
A fiscally transparent partnership's business is carried on by each partner, so a PE of the partnership is a PE of each partner for its share.

A PE starts once the enterprise begins carrying on business through the place, ignoring the time spent setting the place up if that work is substantially different from the place's permanent activity. It ends when the place is disposed of or the activity stops. Temporary interruptions do not end it.

sections.heading: Paragraph 1: working from home or another 'relevant place' (new in 2025)

entries.t: This section covers individuals who, for personal reasons, work for an enterprise from a place in the other State that is neither the enterprise's premises nor a customer's, supplier's or associated enterprise's: a home, second home, holiday rental or a relative's home (an 'other relevant place').
Homes differ from ordinary business premises: other staff usually cannot access them and the individual controls them. The considerations that follow are relevant but not exhaustive.
The facts of the period in question decide. The place must still be 'fixed' under paragraphs 28 to 34, and paragraph 4 still removes places used only for preparatory or auxiliary activities.

An employee using a place for the employer's business does not automatically make it the employer's place of business. Intermittent or incidental work will not, but continuous use over an extended period may, together with other facts.

Key threshold: a home or other relevant place is generally not the enterprise's place of business if the individual works there less than 50 per cent of their total working time for the enterprise over any twelve-month period starting or ending in the fiscal year. Exceptions are not expected in most cases.
Working time is measured by what the individual actually does. Contracts and remote-work policies help only to the extent they match actual conduct.
At or above 50 per cent, the answer depends on the facts and circumstances.

The main factor is whether there is a commercial reason for the work to be done in that State, meaning the individual's physical presence itself helps the business, for example through access to people or resources there. Signs: the enterprise would otherwise rent an office there, or the individual deals directly with customers, suppliers or associated enterprises in a way that being located there makes easier.
No 'productive character' test is needed. If any one of several reasons for using the home is commercial, this factor is met.

Occasional or minor engagement, such as short occasional visits to a customer, is not a commercial reason. The assessment looks at the enterprise's business and how the individual's work fits into it.
Allowing home working only to recruit or keep the individual, or only to save office costs, is not a commercial reason.

Examples of commercial reasons, where physical presence in that State facilitates them: meeting customers; building a customer base or finding opportunities; finding and managing suppliers; real-time service across time zones (call centres, virtual IT or medical support); regular access to relevant expertise, such as university researchers; collaborating with other businesses; services that need presence at the customer's site (training, repairs); and interacting with the enterprise's or associated enterprises' staff. These apply in the same way to associated enterprises as to third parties.
The mere presence of customers, suppliers or associated enterprises in that State, or a different time zone, does not by itself create a commercial reason.
Without a commercial reason, the home is not a place of business of the enterprise unless other facts show otherwise.

It is different where the individual is the only or main person conducting the enterprise's business. A consultant who runs most of her own consulting business for an extended period from a home office in that State has a place of business there.

Five examples. A: three months working from a rental after a holiday is not fixed; recurring use over years is considered in combination, and upkeep costs are irrelevant. B: one or two days a week all year (30 per cent) is fixed but below 50 per cent, so no PE. C: 80 per cent at home plus regular visits to local clients to serve them gives a commercial reason, so a PE. D: 60 per cent at home serving clients remotely, with quarterly visits, gives no commercial reason, so no PE. E: working almost entirely from home to give round-the-clock service to customers in other time zones gives a commercial reason, so a PE.
The list (place of management, branch, office, factory, workshop, mine and so on) gives examples, not an exhaustive list. Each item is a PE only if it meets the paragraph 1 conditions.
'Place of management' is listed separately because it is not necessarily an office. States whose laws have no such separate concept need not mention it.
'any other place of extraction of natural resources' is read broadly and covers all hydrocarbon extraction sites, onshore or offshore.

Exploration is not mentioned, so paragraph 1 governs it. Because States have no common view, they may agree that exploration creates no PE, always creates one, or creates one after a set period. They may instead adopt the free-standing extractive-industries provision in paragraphs 170 to 203.

sections.heading: Paragraph 3: building sites and construction or installation projects

entries.t: A site or project is a PE only if it lasts more than twelve months, even if it contains an office or workshop. An office serving several projects can still be a PE under the general rules if its activities go beyond those in paragraph 4.

The term covers buildings, roads, bridges, canals, renovation that is more than mere maintenance or redecoration, laying pipelines, excavating and dredging, and installing new equipment such as complex machinery. On-site planning and supervision of a building's construction is also covered.

The twelve-month test applies to each site or project separately, ignoring time on unconnected sites. A site that forms a coherent whole commercially and geographically is one unit even if it rests on several contracts.

Splitting contracts among group companies to stay under twelve months can be tackled by domestic anti-avoidance rules or the principal purposes test (Example J in the Commentary on Article 29). States may add an express rule that adds together connected activities of closely related enterprises lasting more than 30 days. Whether activities are connected depends on the facts.

A site exists from the start of the contractor's work in the country, including preparatory work such as a planning office. It continues until the work is finished or permanently abandoned. Testing time and temporary interruptions (weather, seasonal factors, shortages) count, and subcontractors' time counts towards the general contractor's period.
For a fiscally transparent partnership, the period is measured at partnership level, so each partner has a PE for its share however little time it spends on site.
Projects that move continuously, such as roads, canals or pipelines, are still one project, applying the coherence principles of paragraphs 22 to 25.

Paragraph 4 lists activities that do not create a PE when carried on through a fixed place, but only if they are preparatory or auxiliary. Because subparagraph e) covers any other such activity, the paragraph works as a general limit on paragraph 1. Combinations under f) are covered only if the overall activity is preparatory or auxiliary, and paragraph 4.1 adds an anti-fragmentation rule.

The decisive test is whether the place's activity is itself an essential and significant part of the enterprise's activity as a whole. A place whose general purpose is the same as the whole enterprise's is never preparatory or auxiliary.

Preparatory activities are done in contemplation of the core activity and are often short, though not always (for example, training staff before sending them to remote sites). Auxiliary activities support the core without being part of it. An activity needing a significant share of the enterprise's assets or employees is unlikely to be auxiliary.
Subparagraphs a) to e) cover activities for the enterprise itself. Doing them for others, such as storing other people's goods, can create a PE.

A) Storage, display or delivery of the enterprise's own goods is assessed against its business model. A large warehouse with many staff delivering goods sold online is not auxiliary where delivery is a core function. A fruit exporter's specialised bonded warehouse used only to store fruit during customs clearance can be.

Cables and pipelines: the owner or operator carrying other enterprises' property cannot rely on a) or e). An oil refiner whose pipeline only carries its own oil across a country to its refinery can rely on a). Customers who merely buy transport or transmission do not have the pipeline at their disposal.

B) A stock of goods kept by a third party at its own premises does not put a place at the enterprise's disposal. Otherwise the preparatory or auxiliary test applies, whether storage happens before or after the sale.
C) Goods processed by another enterprise: a toll manufacturer's premises where the enterprise's goods are stored for processing are not at the enterprise's disposal.
D) Purchasing will usually not qualify where buying the goods is a core function of a business that sells them. Examples contrast core buying offices with incidental ones.
D) Collecting information (added in 2017) is usually auxiliary, for example an investment fund's office gathering information, but not where gathering information is the business itself.

E) covers any other preparatory or auxiliary activity: advertising, supplying information, scientific research, servicing patents or know-how. It does not cover supplying plans developed for a particular customer, research that turns into manufacturing, patent servicing where that is the business itself, or any management function, even for part of the enterprise or group.
An office whose staff take an active part in negotiating important parts of sales contracts is not preparatory or auxiliary.

Paragraph 4 restricts paragraph 1. Unless paragraph 4.1 applies, subparagraph f) is irrelevant where several fixed places are each used only for preparatory or auxiliary activities: each is assessed separately.

The exception lasts only while the activity stays preparatory or auxiliary. It also covers disposing of the place's movable property, such as selling displayed goods at the end of a trade fair, but not goods that were never displayed. A place that also carries on non-exempt activities is a single PE for both.

Alternative wording is offered for States that regard some listed activities as inherently preparatory or auxiliary. They can drop the condition for those activities and rely on paragraph 4.1 against abuse.

Paragraph 4.1 stops an enterprise, or closely related enterprises, from splitting a cohesive operation into small pieces that each look preparatory or auxiliary. It applies where complementary functions are carried on in the same State and either one of the places is a PE or the combined activity is not preparatory or auxiliary.
Whether enterprises are closely related is tested under paragraph 8.

Examples. A bank's office verifying loan applications is complementary to its branches, which are PEs. A parent's small warehouse supplies goods sold through its subsidiary's local store: because the store is a PE of the subsidiary and the functions are complementary, the warehouse loses the exception. A further example contrasts places whose functions are not complementary.

A person acting for an enterprise can create a PE whether or not they are an employee and whether or not they are resident or have premises in that State. It would go too far to let any such person do so, so the paragraph limits this to persons who habitually conclude contracts, or play the principal role leading to them, and who are not independent agents.

Conditions: the person acts in the State on behalf of the enterprise; habitually concludes contracts, or habitually plays the principal role leading to contracts routinely concluded without material modification by the enterprise; and the contracts are in the enterprise's name, transfer ownership or use of its property, or are for services it provides.
Even then there is no PE if the person is an independent agent under paragraph 6, or if the activities are limited to those in paragraph 4.
'On behalf of' means involving the enterprise in business activities to a particular extent, as an agent or commissionaire does. A distributor buying and reselling on its own account does not.

'Concludes contracts' follows contract law. A contract can be concluded without signature, for example by accepting an offer, and negotiating all elements in the State can count even if the contract is signed elsewhere.

'Principal role' catches cases where the contract is the direct result of the person's actions in the State even though contract law says it was concluded elsewhere, typically by the person who convinces the customer. Routine approval by the enterprise does not change that. Promotion that does not directly produce contracts, such as pharmaceutical representatives encouraging doctors to prescribe, is not covered.

Example: a subsidiary's staff persuade large local clients to buy a foreign group company's products, quoting its fixed prices and standard terms, which they cannot change. The clients then conclude the contracts online with the foreign company. The staff play the principal role, so the foreign company has a PE.

The wording covers contracts legally binding on the enterprise and contracts it will in fact perform even though someone else is the formal party, as in commissionaire structures. 'In the name of' is not read literally. For b) and c), the key is that the person acts for the enterprise, whose property or services are the subject of the contracts.
For b), it does not matter whether the property already existed or belonged to the enterprise when the contract was concluded.
A person who sells on its own behalf and then sources goods or services from other enterprises (even associated ones) to perform its obligations is not acting on behalf of those suppliers.
Only contracts relating to the enterprise's business proper count. Internal contracts, such as hiring staff, do not.

'Habitually' requires repetition rather than isolated cases, depending on the nature of the contracts and the business. No precise frequency test exists, but the factors in paragraphs 28 to 30 are relevant.

When the conditions are met, the PE extends to everything the person does for the enterprise, not only the contract work. Persons who do not meet the conditions cannot create an agency PE, although paragraph 1 can still apply to a place at the enterprise's disposal.
Rights under the contracts may be allocated to the deemed PE, but not all profits from performing them: Article 7 governs attribution, taking account of work done by others.

Business carried on through an independent agent acting in the ordinary course of its business creates no PE. The exception covers only persons acting as independent agents in their own business, not employees acting for their employer or partners acting for their partnership. Article 15 guidance helps tell employment from independent services.

Independence depends on the agent's obligations to the enterprise. Detailed instructions or comprehensive control mean the agent is not legally independent, and economic independence (bearing business risk) also matters.
A subsidiary that does not fall under the 'exclusively for related enterprises' rule must still pass the general independence tests.

An independent agent answers for results but not for how it works. Limits on the scale of business affect only the scope of authority. Giving the principal a lot of information is not a sign of dependence unless it is done to seek approval for how the business is conducted.

Acting for one principal over a long period makes independence less likely but is not decisive. The question is whether the agent runs an autonomous business with its own risk and reward. Several principals acting together to control the agent can also mean dependence.
Activities unrelated to the agency business, such as acting as a distributor on its own account, are not part of the ordinary course of the agency business.

A person acting exclusively or almost exclusively for closely related enterprises is not independent. As a guide, sales for unrelated enterprises below 10 per cent of the agent's sales mean 'almost exclusively'. Because of this rule and the definition of 'closely related', a subsidiary acting as agent only for its group will generally not qualify.

Foreign insurers can do large-scale business through agencies without meeting paragraph 1 or 5. Many pre-2017 treaties therefore deem a PE where premiums are collected or risks insured through a dependent agent. Whether to include such a rule depends on each State's situation.
A subsidiary is not, in itself, a PE of its parent. It is a separate legal entity, and control alone does not change that.

A parent can still have a PE under paragraph 1 if the subsidiary's premises are at the parent's disposal and used for the parent's own business, subject to paragraphs 3 and 4. It can also have one under paragraph 5 if the subsidiary acts as its dependent agent, unless paragraph 6 applies.
The same applies to any group company. The test is applied company by company, so one group company's PE says nothing about another's.
A group company that provides services, such as management services, to another group company from its own premises with its own staff does not put those premises at the recipient's disposal.

Persons are closely related if, on all the facts, one controls the other or both are under common control. This is automatically met where one holds, directly or indirectly, more than 50 per cent of the other's beneficial interest (for a company, votes and value of shares), or where a third person holds more than 50 per cent of both.

Computer equipment at a location can be a PE, but the equipment must be distinguished from the data and software it runs. A website is not tangible, so it has no location that can be a place of business.

A website hosted on an internet service provider's server does not put the server at the enterprise's disposal, even if the enterprise chose the server or its location. If the enterprise owns or leases and operates the server, the server's location can be a PE.
A server must be fixed (in one place for long enough), and the business must be carried on through it. No personnel are needed if the equipment performs the functions itself.

There is no PE where the server's functions are only preparatory or auxiliary (communications links, advertising, mirroring for security, gathering market data, supplying information). For hosting providers, hosting is the core business. For an online retailer, a server that concludes contracts, processes payments and delivers products automatically performs core functions.
An internet service provider hosting a site will generally not be a dependent agent of the enterprise.

sections.heading: Taxation of services and the optional services PE

entries.t: Under Articles 5 and 7 together, profits from services are taxed at source only if attributable to a PE.
Administrative and compliance reasons favour residence taxation of services that are not attributable to a PE.
Some States disagree. They think services performed in their territory should be taxable there, point out that some service businesses need no fixed place, and worry about gaps in their domestic law.
All members agree that a State should not tax services performed outside its territory, that tax should be on profits rather than gross payments, and that a minimal presence should not trigger tax.
The Committee therefore limited when States that want source taxation should have it: only services performed in their territory, and only the profits from them.

Optional wording: an enterprise is deemed to have a PE if (a) an individual performing its services is present more than 183 days in any twelve-month period and those services produce more than 50 per cent of its active gross revenues, or (b) it performs services for more than 183 days in twelve months for the same or connected projects through individuals present in the State.
The provision extends the PE definition and only deems a PE where none would otherwise exist.

It applies notwithstanding the construction-site rule. Using the same period in both rules avoids practical overlap for a single site, but a project spread across a country can trigger a deemed PE even if no individual site reaches the construction threshold. Some States may prefer the construction rule to prevail.
Only services are covered, not other activities. They must be supplied by the enterprise to third parties and performed in the State.
The individuals counted are those through whom the enterprise carries on business (paragraph 39): employees and others taking its instructions.

Subparagraph a) targets mainly single-person enterprises. It needs more than 183 days of presence and more than 50 per cent of active gross revenues from services performed in the State through that individual. Examples follow.

Subparagraph b) counts days on which services are performed for the same or connected projects, seen from the enterprise's perspective. 'Connected' covers separate contracts that are commercially linked.

An individual's services count for another enterprise only if that enterprise supervises, directs or controls the work. Services delivered through an outsourcing provider's staff do not count for the contracting company, whether or not the provider is associated. Examples follow.
Splitting activities to stay under 183 days can be tackled by anti-avoidance rules, the principal purposes test, or a specific provision.
Activities deemed carried on through the PE allow the State to tax under Article 7, but only the profits from performing those services.
The provision does not apply where the services are limited to paragraph 4 activities. Since it concerns services to others, most of paragraph 4 will rarely be relevant.

sections.heading: Optional provision for extractive industries (new in 2025)

entries.t: This optional, free-standing article for oil, gas and mining activities sets a lower PE threshold: a deemed PE once a non-resident has operated in the State for longer than a bilaterally agreed period. It is modelled on existing treaties.

Resource-rich States want an adequate share of the value of finite resources. Royalties, contracts and other tools are outside this Commentary, which assumes the States have agreed to extend source taxation.
States against the provision point to compliance costs and the difficulty of attributing profits to short-lived PEs. The balance is a matter for negotiation.

Some States want only offshore coverage, since onshore mines will usually be PEs anyway. Others want onshore too, to capture short engineering, consultancy or seismic-survey work that would otherwise fall below the threshold.

Provision text, summarised: it applies notwithstanding Articles 5 and 13 and defines 'relevant activity' in offshore-only and offshore-and-onshore versions. It deems a PE once relevant activities exceed an agreed aggregate period in any twelve months. The source State may also tax gains on resource-related immovable property (including exploration and exploitation rights), on movable property of such a PE, and on shares or comparable interests that derived more than 50 per cent of their value from that property at any time in the 365 days before sale.
The provision overrides Articles 5 and 13 where they would block source taxation. Taxing rights the source State already has under those Articles are kept.

'Relevant activity': 'offshore' means a State's internal and territorial waters and the areas where it has sovereign rights over the seabed. 'In connection with' brings in related services. Offshore, everything connected with exploration and exploitation is covered except listed vessel activities.
Onshore, only 'specialised' related services are covered, meaning services needing expertise or equipment specific to the sector. A caterer serving many industries in the same way is not covered.
Supply and personnel transport, towing, anchor handling and other auxiliary vessels are excluded. This exclusion is wider than the international traffic rule in Article 8.

All stages are covered: exploration, development, production and decommissioning. Only non-renewable resources count (hydrocarbons, metals, minerals), not wind, solar or hydro. Paragraph 4 activities are not carved out.

Once the period is exceeded, all relevant activities are deemed carried on through a PE, regardless of the customer or project. Profits are attributed under Article 7 and the residence State gives relief under Article 23.
The period is negotiated: existing treaties use 30, 90 or 183 days, among others. 'In the other Contracting State' should be clarified to include areas of sovereign rights over the seabed.
There is no built-in anti-contract-splitting rule, but optional wording is offered, mainly for States without the principal purposes test. It uses the 'closely related' definition from Article 5(8).

Gains: the source State gets the primary right. Exploration and exploitation rights count as immovable property, movable property of the PE is covered, and share-sale gains apply a 50 per cent value test over the prior 365 days that adds together both types of property.

Optionally, source taxation of employees working on relevant activities can be extended beyond Article 15, for example through a separate rule or a shorter day count in Article 15(2)(a). States should weigh the administrative burden, and States using the exemption method should avoid double non-taxation, for example by switching to the credit method.

membersNote: Paragraphs 204 to 227 are members' observations on this Commentary and paragraphs 228 to 259 are their reservations on the Article. Non-OECD economies' positions are in section P(5). Those relevant to the treaty you selected appear in the Other countries tab.
